1:
The psalm carries the strangest of headings, and the witnesses linger over it before a word of the prayer is read. "Shiggaion of David, which he sang unto the LORD, concerning the words of Cush the Benjamite" — the title itself divides them. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry takes Shiggaion for a song, either "a wandering song" whose several parts differ in matter and composition yet are artfully joined, or "a charming song" delightful to sing; and he marks that David not only penned it but sang it to the Lord in a devout and cheerful spirit, his harp untouched by one jarring string though he had been basely abused. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke traces the word to shagah, to wander, and reads it as a wandering song composed in David's flight from Saul, or, with Bishop Horsley, a "wandering ode" that shifts subject and style from part to part, perhaps even an unpremeditated improviso.

Over Cush the witnesses openly contend. Henry and Clarke suspect a veiled name for Saul himself — Clarke noting that Cush is unknown to Jewish history and is likely "a name of disguise" for the son of Kish, the Benjamite king whose persecution the psalm fits better than any other episode; Henry, that Saul's barbarous usage bespoke him rather a Cushite or Ethiopian than a true-born Israelite, though he thinks it more likely some kinsman of Saul named Cush. The reformed John Calvin flatly refuses the disguise: the fictitious-name theory rests on no sufficient argument, for David names Saul openly and paints him as darkly elsewhere, so why suppress the name here? Cush was a real man, one of Saul's kinsmen and fellow-tribesmen, the author or instrument of the slander that inflamed the whole people against him. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch agree that Cush was an actual Benjamite of the persecution, and note how the superscription, with its deliberate "concerning the words," points to the slanderous sayings that occasioned the song.

The latin-fathers voice reads the title another way still: Augustine, taking the very names spiritually, interprets Chusi as "silence" and finds in the whole heading "a veil of mysteries" to be lifted once the reader has passed over to Christ. When the prayer itself begins — "O LORD my God, in thee do I put my trust" — the schools converge. Gill and Calvin both stress the tense: not that David had trusted or would trust, but that he does trust, a confidence held fast and unbroken in the very thick of his affliction, for this, Calvin says, is faith's genuine proof, to persevere in hope when visited with adversity. Clarke hears in "Jehovah my God" the strongest confidence the soul can frame; the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the clause "in thee have I taken refuge"; and Gill grounds the following cry, "save me... and deliver me," in the covenant bond that makes God at once his God and his shield.
2:
The poet's dread, hitherto spread over many enemies, now narrows to a single figure who has made himself conspicuous, and the witnesses mark the sudden shift from plural persecutors to one — "lest he tear my soul like a lion." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes this change from plural to singular as characteristic of the Psalms, and hears in the lion a reminiscence of the beasts David had faced in his youth, the lion and the bear of his shepherd days (1 Sam. 17:37), the same predatory image that returns at Ps. 3:7. He observes too that the Septuagint, followed by the Vulgate and Syriac, take the verb in its primitive sense of "snatch away," so that the line becomes, as Milton rendered it, "tearing, and no rescue nigh."

The reformed John Gill identifies the lion as the chief of David's persecutors, Saul himself, likened to the beast for his royal majesty, his power, and above all his wrath, which, unleashed, would rend the psalmist's very soul from his body; and he sets beside it the apostle's word that names a Roman ruler a lion (2 Tim. 4:17) and Peter's warning of the adversary who goes about as a roaring lion (1 Pet. 5:8). The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke presses the aptness of the figure to Saul: as the lion is king in the forest, so was Saul king over the land; as the lion seizes and tears his prey at once, so David expected to be seized and suddenly destroyed by the king who had already hurled a javelin at him. From the paw of such a beast no creature of the forest could be delivered, and David knew Saul's power to be as irresistible, with none among his friends able to rescue him from those hands.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the verse together with the protestation that follows, taking the demonstrative "this" of the next line to point back to the substance of the Benjamite's slanders; and they draw a fine contrast between the heightened poetry here and the plain prose of David's own words to Saul, "there is no evil in mine hand" (1 Sam. 24:11). The witnesses do not divide: whether the lion be named as Saul or left as the type of every ravening foe, they agree that the image measures at once the ferocity of the danger and the helplessness of the hunted, who has, as the verse ends, none to deliver.
3:
Turning from his fear to his conscience, the psalmist begins a solemn protestation of innocence, staking everything on a conditional oath — "O LORD my God, if I have done this." The reformed John Gill explains that "this" needs no naming because the charge was public knowledge: that David had lain in wait for Saul and sought his life; and he records the Targum's turn, which refers the words to the psalm itself, "if I have made this song with an evil intention," to blacken another with false charges. The wesleyan-arminian voices fill in the accusation. Adam Clarke recalls that David was charged with affecting the kingdom and waiting to take the life of his king, patron, and friend; and in his appeal to God he meets these charges with indignation, calling down curse and calamity on himself if he had ever meditated such a thing. John Wesley glosses the "iniquity in my hands" as the deeds "which Cush and others falsely lay to my charge," the iniquity lying in his actions.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott ties the verse tightly to history, taking "this" as the Benjamite's slander and pointing to the two famous occasions when David spared Saul — comparing 1 Sam. 24:11 and still more 1 Sam. 26:18 — as showing how closely the psalm is bound to those instances of his magnanimous and generous conduct toward the king. Keil and Delitzsch, reading the same clause, again set the poetry beside the prose, hearing behind "if there be iniquity in my hands" the plain protest David had made to Saul with his own lips.

The puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon draws out the weight of such an oath. So far from hiding treasonable designs in his hands or ungratefully requiting a friend, David had twice let his enemy escape when he lay wholly in his power — once in the cave and again in the sleeping camp — and could therefore make his appeal to heaven with a clear conscience; yet Spurgeon calls the imprecation a most solemn one, justifiable only by the extremity of the occasion, and warns the reader against trifling with such appeals to the dread tribunal of God. The witnesses agree that no innocence can shield a man from the calumnies of the wicked, and that when men falsely accuse us it is a great comfort if our own hearts acquit us, so that we may lodge the appeal with the God who tries the reins.
4:
The oath runs on, and its second half turns the accusation inside out: not only had David done no evil to the man at peace with him, he had actually returned good for evil. The reformed John Gill reads "him that was at peace with me" of Saul in the days before the breach, when David lived at his court and ate at his table and formed no plot against his crown or life; and he notes Jarchi's alternative rendering, "if I rewarded him as he rewarded me, evil for evil" — a thing David did not do, and which, Gill adds, is eminently true of Christ his antitype and binding on every believer. The wesleyan-arminian witnesses point to the deed behind the boast. Adam Clarke recalls the cave, where God's providence put Saul's life into David's hand and he contented himself with cutting off the skirt of the robe, merely to show the king the danger he had escaped and the spirit of the man he hunted; and even for that his heart smote him, as an indignity to the Lord's anointed. John Wesley likewise glosses "I have delivered" of the moment "when it was in my power to destroy him."

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the verse as, "on the contrary, so far from returning evil for good, I have returned good for evil," with little doubt that it alludes to those same incidents. But he also flags a real difficulty in the text: on metrical grounds, and to smooth the abrupt change of construction, Ewald conjectured that two clauses had dropped out, and Ellicott reports the Septuagint and Vulgate as supporting the suspicion of corruption, a very slight change yielding the probable sense, "if I have returned evil to him that dealt friendly with me, and injured my enemy without cause." He even sets down Milton's rendering — "if I have wrought ill to him that meant me peace... and not freed my foe for nought" — as catching yet another colour of the disputed lines.

The witnesses do not divide over the substance. Whether the text stand as received or be mended after the ancient versions, they agree that David's plea is the plea of a man who had twice held his persecutor's life in his hand and twice let it go, and who therefore dares to submit the whole matter to a God who cannot be deceived, asking to be judged by the very magnanimity his enemies had twisted into a crime.
5:
Having sworn his innocence, the psalmist seals the oath with a fearful self-imprecation: if the charge be true, "let the enemy persecute my soul, and take it." The reformed John Gill reads it as a plain condition — if the things laid against him could be proved, then let David content himself that Saul his enemy should pursue him, apprehend him, and take away his life. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke puts it as bluntly: "if I have been guilty of the things laid to my charge, let the worst evils fall upon me."

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott mines the Hebrew for the force of the curse. "Let the enemy" is better "let an enemy"; the verb rendered "persecute" is literally to "burn," a hot pursuit; "tread down" is the word used of a potter treading his clay (Isa. 41:25), of horses trampling (Ezek. 26:11), of a herd trampling its pasture. The "dust" he links to the "dust of death" of Ps. 22:15, and "mine honour" he takes, by the parallelism, to mean the soul or life itself, as where the Authorized Version renders the same word "glory" in Ps. 16:9 and Ps. 57:8. To lay one's honour in the dust, he adds, is in any case a common figure of utter abasement, and he quotes Shakespeare's "thy glory droopeth to the dust" to illustrate the phrase.

At the close stands the word "Selah," and the witnesses treat it as the commentators are wont to. Ellicott takes it here for a direction to the music — one of the places, he says, that suggest reading it as a signal for the players to strike up with passion and force, marking the solemnity of so dreadful an appeal. The puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon, weighing the same pause, sees David enhancing the solemnity of his oath by the customary rest, and draws the lesson that we should let our yea be yea and our nay nay, since to a true heart a simple word is as binding as another man's oath. The witnesses do not divide: the verse is the extremity of a clear conscience, a man so sure of his innocence that he will consent, if he lies, to be hunted down, trampled into the earth, and laid with his very glory in the dust — and then, at "Selah," bids the music hold the terrible thought a moment before the prayer resumes.
6:
From protest the psalm turns to petition, and the cry grows suddenly bold — "Arise, O LORD, in thine anger." The reformed John Gill is careful that such language ascribes no local motion to God, who is infinite and immense, but speaks after the manner of men: God seems at times to lie down unconcerned with human affairs, careless of the insults of the wicked and the oppression of the righteous, and the psalmist begs him to "arise" — to come forth in power for his people — and to arise "in anger," showing his displeasure by letting his enemies feel the weight of his hand. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears David pleading his enemies' wrath as the ground for God's: "Lord, they are unjustly angry at me, be thou justly angry with them"; and he notes that the word rendered "rage" is plural — the furies, the outrages, of many foes — so that those need not fear men's wrath who have God's wrath for them.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears in the quick, abrupt succession of ejaculations the very excitement of the poet's mind. "Because of the rage" he would render "against the rage"; he records the Septuagint and Vulgate reading "in the ends of," which Jerome explained as "exalt thyself by making an end of my enemies," and the Syriac "be thou lifted up upon the necks of my enemies"; and he arranges the last line as two petitions — "yea, awake for me; prepare the judgment" — preferring the imperatives to the past tense for the parallelism's sake. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley glosses "lift up thyself" as "glorify thyself, and show thyself to be above them," and takes "the judgment thou hast commanded" for the righteous sentence God had already appointed and declared by the prophet Samuel.

The puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon feels the daring of the words most keenly. To bid the Lord "awake" implies not merely inactivity but sleep, and can be said of God only in a very limited sense, for he never slumbers, though he often seems to while the wicked prevail and the saints are trodden in the dust; that silence, Spurgeon says, is the patience of longsuffering, borne cheerfully in the hope that sinners may be led to repentance. The witnesses do not divide: the boldness is the boldness of faith, which may rouse the sleeping Judge precisely because it knows the judgment has long since been commanded.
7:
The petition now widens from David's single cause to a whole assembly gathered about the throne — "so shall the congregation of the people compass thee about." The reformed John Gill takes the congregation for the nation of Israel, the twelve tribes, and sets aside the reading of some Jewish commentators who make the encompassing a hostile one, as though the people surrounded David to seize him, and so, since David was dear to God as the apple of his eye, compassed God himself. Rather, Gill hears the tribes surrounding the altar with songs of deliverance when David is at last rid of his enemies and raised to the throne. The wesleyan-arminian witnesses read "return thou on high" of God ascending the judgment-seat: Adam Clarke pictures the faithful of the land full of gloomy apprehension, their minds divided as they hear the charges against David, and prays God to mount the tribunal and let all see who is innocent and who guilty; John Wesley has the people come from all parts to worship, and takes "high" of the tribunal set up on high above the throng.

The grammatical-historical witnesses lift the verse toward a vision of universal judgment. Charles Ellicott renders it "let the communities of peoples be gathered round thee," and "for their sakes" rather "over it" or "above it": Jehovah summons the nations, arranges them at his tribunal, and then returns to his high throne to preside — a picture of arraigned nations that Ellicott thinks favours reading the psalm as the voice of the community rather than of a single man. Keil and Delitzsch hear the calm language of courageous trust rising and subsiding in the verse, and make the great observation that "this Psalm is the key to all Psalms which contain prayers against one's enemies," since its plea is directed not against the individuals as such but against the wickedness that is in them.

Here the witnesses genuinely differ over the scene. Is the "return on high" God's withdrawal to the throne as a victor after battle, or in proof of his supremacy as judge — readings Ellicott expressly weighs and sets against his own — or the simpler homage of a delivered people gathering to praise? Gill, Clarke, and Wesley keep the individual David and his worshipping nation in view; Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch see the assembled peoples of the earth before the seat of judgment. The witnesses do not quarrel over the truth that God will mount the seat; they divide only over how wide the congregation stands that waits for him to do so.
8:
With the court now seated, the psalmist presses for a verdict upon himself — "the LORD shall judge the people: judge me, O LORD, according to my righteousness." The reformed John Gill takes the first clause of God as Judge of all the earth, who judges the world in righteousness and pleads the cause of his own; and on that ground David, suiting his suit to the Judge's character, asks to be judged according to his righteousness and the sincerity of his heart. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads "judge me" as "let my innocence be brought to the light, and my just dealing made clear as the noonday." The puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon sees David, his hand upon an honest heart and his cry to a righteous Judge, drawing near as the heralds proclaim the court open, and pleading his integrity in the matter at variance between himself and Saul.

But the plea raises a real question, and the witnesses divide over how a sinner may ask to be judged by his own righteousness. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott records Jerome's verdict that "David could not say this; this properly belongs to the Saviour, who was sinless," and reports the further opinion of others that it is the ideal Israel which stands before the tribunal; yet Ellicott himself, comparing Job's protestations of innocence and persistent demand for a trial, judges that David refers naturally to his innocence of the calumny brought against him, his conduct as between Saul and himself having been blameless. So the sides are drawn: some refer the plea to Christ alone, in whom no fault was found; some to the ideal people of God; and some, with Gill and Clarke and Spurgeon, to David's relative and particular innocence of the charge — not a claim to sinless perfection but to a clear conscience in this cause.

The reformed voice keeps both truths in view, for Gill can plead David's integrity in the affair with Saul while confessing that only in Christ could any man call heaven to attest his uprightness in all things. The witnesses do not finally divide over the fact that God will judge righteously; they differ only over whose righteousness the verse dares to name — the spotless righteousness of the Redeemer, the vindicated cause of the church, or the honest heart of a persecuted man who asks no more than to be cleared of a lie. And all agree that to submit one's cause to the Judge of all the earth is safe precisely because he will do right, and none can gainsay his sentence.
9:
David's prayer now broadens from his own cause to the moral order of the world: "Oh let the wickedness of the wicked come to an end." The reformed John Gill hears in it more than a wish against particular foes; the wickedness of the wicked will not truly end until the measure of it is full and the wicked are no more, in that new Jerusalem state where there shall be no Canaanite in the house of the Lord and no sinner in the new earth. He notes the alternative rendering, "let wickedness now consume the wicked," as in the end it will, unless the grace of God prevent; but by this petition, whatever its reach, David expresses his hatred of sin and his love of righteousness. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the two clauses as the double desire of every believer — the destruction of sin and the perpetuity of righteousness: that corruption may be mortified in ourselves and others, and that the good may be confirmed and made better, established against the wiles and malice of the wicked.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps the plea concrete: "the wickedness of the wicked" is the iniquity of Saul's conduct, and "establish the just" is a prayer that the people may see David's uprightness. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders "establish" literally, "let him stand erect," and turns the ground of the petition into a direct address — "thou trier of hearts and reins, thou just God" — noting that the verb for "try" is the word used of assaying metals in the furnace (Ps. 12:6; Prov. 17:3).

On that closing plea the witnesses gather as one. The puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon calls it the universal longing of the whole company of the elect, that they may at last be delivered from the filthy conversation of the wicked; and he marvels at the weight of the last sentence — how deep, how strict, how intimate the divine search that tries "the hearts," the secret thoughts, "and reins," the inward affections, so that all things are naked and open to the eyes of him with whom we have to do. Because the righteous God so tries the reins, Henry adds, he knows the secret wickedness of the wicked and how to bring it to an end, and is witness to the secret sincerity of the just and has hidden ways of establishing it. The witnesses do not divide: the prayer against evil rests wholly on the character of the God who reads the heart, and who alone can both consume the wickedness of the wicked and confirm the standing of the just.
10:
With the tenth verse the psalm's temper changes from petition to settled confidence, and the witnesses feel the calm come over it — "my defence is of God, which saveth the upright in heart." The reformed John Gill weighs the Hebrew, "my shield is in" or "of" or "with God," and reads it of God himself as David's shield, his protector and defender; or, more mystically, of Christ the shield of faith, who was with God from all eternity as his Word and Son and is with him still as the intercessor who pleads his people's cause. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, opening here the long meditation that carries to the psalm's end, hears David resolve to look for shelter in no other: "if I have defence, it must be of God," whose name is a strong tower (Prov. 18:10). On this confidence Henry builds two pillars — the particular favour God bears to all who are sincere, for he saves the upright in heart with an everlasting salvation, and the general respect he has for justice, since God judges the righteous and will maintain every righteous cause.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the verse as David laying down his weapons: "I now leave my cause in the hands of my Judge; I have no uneasy or fearful apprehensions, because I know God will save the upright in heart." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes the marginal sense, "my shield is upon God," comparing the like Hebrew of Ps. 62:7, where God is, as it were, the shield-bearer of his servant, and cites Milton's rendering that casts the whole defence on the God "who both just and wise, saves the upright at heart at last."

The puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon hears the note of triumph in it: the judge has heard the cause and cleared the guiltless, and yonder stands the slandered one with his harp, hymning the justice of his Lord. "Oh, how good to have a true and upright heart"; the filth flung by base hands will not long abide on the white garments of the saints, but shall be brushed off by providence, to the vexation of those who threw it. Keil and Delitzsch, looking to the verses just ahead, add the note of warning that balances the comfort: if God will one day let his wrath break forth, he does not do it without giving daily threatenings beforehand to the ungodly (Isa. 66:14), to strike a wholesome terror into them. The witnesses do not divide: the upright in heart are safe, and may know themselves safe, under the shield that is God himself.
11:
The confidence just expressed rests on a twofold truth about God as Judge, and it is the second half that sets the witnesses at odds — "God judgeth the righteous, and God is angry with the wicked every day." The reformed John Gill takes the first clause of God governing and protecting the truly righteous, those made righteous by the obedience of Christ, and allows the rendering "God is a righteous Judge," who is such now in his government of the world and will be such in the general judgment. On the second clause the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry dwells without hesitation: the wicked are children of wrath, and God is angry with them every day, his anger new every morning as his mercies are new to his people, for they are every day doing what provokes him; he is angry with them even in their most prosperous and merriest days, so that if they prosper it is in wrath, and if they pray their very prayers are an abomination. John Wesley adds the sharp point that God is angry "even then, when his providence seems to favour them, and they are most secure."

But the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke halts over the very words and mounts a long textual case against them. The Hebrew, he shows, says simply "and God is angry every day," the added "with the wicked" being borrowed from the Chaldee; and he marshals version after version — Vulgate, Septuagint, Syriac, Arabic, Aethiopic, Coverdale — that render it as a question or a negation, "will he be angry every day?" or "not bringing forth his anger every day." The whole difficulty, he says, turns on a single word: el, pointed one way, means "God," but the same letters pointed another way mean "not," so that the true sense may be "God judgeth the righteous, and is not angry every day" — not always chiding, but longsuffering under the continual wickedness of men.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reports the same proposal — to read "and not" for "and God," in conformity with the ancient versions — but judges it unnecessary, keeping the received text, "God is a righteous judge, and God avengeth every day." So the debate is real and unresolved: whether the line proclaims a God angry with the wicked every day, or a God who, though a righteous judge, is not angry every day but patient and slow to wrath. The witnesses divide over the word, yet not over the doctrine beneath it, that the same God who saves the upright is the settled and righteous enemy of impenitent sin.
12:
The warning to the wicked now arms itself, and the witnesses watch God, as it were, take up his weapons against the man who will not repent — "if he turn not, he will whet his sword." The reformed John Gill is careful about the subject: it is not God who must turn but the enemy, the wicked man, who unless he is converted and changed in heart and life stands under the whetted blade; and he notes that the Septuagint, Vulgate, Arabic, and Ethiopic read "if ye turn not," an apostrophe to the wicked at large. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke observes that the Syriac joins the clause to the previous verse, and reports the reading of some who take the two verses together — "God is a just Judge... if the sinner turn not, he will whet his sword; he hath bent his bow, and made it ready" — which, he thinks, gives the true sense of both. John Wesley reads the coming stroke as God's own: "he will hasten, and speedily execute his judgments upon him."

The grammatical-historical witnesses attend to the idiom and the archery. Charles Ellicott calls the opening doubly idiomatic and would render it "surely, he will again whet his sword," the verb "turn" carrying the sense of repetition; and he notes that "bent" is literally "trodden," the foot being used, as by archers still, to bend the great bow. Keil and Delitzsch, taking the whole closing strophe together, read it as the sentence the judge pronounces upon the enemy of God, and they too weigh the disputed verb, preferring "if a man does not repent, then Jahve will whet his sword" (Deut. 32:41) against the rendering "he will again whet," which they find meaningless in the connection.

Beneath the small grammatical differences the witnesses hold one picture in common. Judgment is being prepared, not sprung; the sword is in the whetting and the bow in the drawing, and all the while a space is left for the sinner to turn. Henry, expounding these verses, had already drawn the mercy hidden in the menace: the threatening is introduced with a gracious proviso, "if he turn not," so that the man who repents shall find his sin pardoned and all made well, and the destruction of sinners may still be prevented by their conversion. The witnesses do not divide: the God who bends the bow is slow to loose the arrow, and every day of delay is a day of warning to the impenitent to lay down his enmity before the string is let go.
13:
The armoury of divine justice is now fully laid out, and the witnesses count the weapons — "he hath also prepared for him the instruments of death; he ordaineth his arrows against the persecutors." The reformed John Gill takes the instruments of death for the weapons of God's indignation, issuing in both the first death and the second: diseases, famine, and pestilence for the body, and for the soul that death of which the law is the minister and the very gospel, to wicked men, becomes a savour of death unto death; and the devils themselves, Gill adds, will be the executioners of that final sentence. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads "him" of the wicked man and "ordaineth" as designs or fits for this very use, marking that of all sinners persecutors are set up as the fairest marks of divine wrath: they set God at defiance, but cannot set themselves out of the reach of his judgments.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, still unfolding the passage, lingers over the variety of the instruments, all of which breathe threatening and slaughter — a sword to wound and kill at hand, and a bow and arrows to strike down at a distance those who think to flee beyond the reach of vindictive justice, so that if the sinner escape the iron weapon the bow of steel shall strike him through (Job 20:24). Yet these instruments, Henry insists, though made ready and always at hand, are not hastily used: while God is preparing them he gives the sinner timely warning and space to repent, being slow to punish and unwilling that any should perish; and the longer the destruction is delayed to leave room for repentance, the sorer it will fall if that space be not improved.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott turns to the last phrase, "against the persecutors," which he renders literally "for those burning": the meaning, he thinks, is that God makes his arrows into fiery arrows, tipped with flame by wrapping them in burning tow, the very custom that lies behind the "fiery darts" of Eph. 6:16 and Milton's "rattling storm of arrows barb'd with fire." Here one voice reads the verse more narrowly than the rest: the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears in it a specific prophecy of the tragical death of Saul, who was wounded by the arrows of the Philistines and fell at last upon his own sword. The witnesses do not divide over the substance — that God has weapons enough for every impenitent foe — though Clarke alone reads the arrows as pointing straight to the king's own end on Gilboa.
14:
The psalm now traces the wicked man's undoing to the malice teeming within him, and the witnesses take up its startling figure of a monstrous birth — "behold, he travaileth with iniquity, and hath conceived mischief, and brought forth falsehood." The reformed John Gill reads it of a man so full of iniquity, so big with it as a woman with child, that he is in pain until he brings it forth in act. The wesleyan-arminian witnesses press the image on the calumniator. Adam Clarke sees in it the very pitch of Saul's envy, wrath, and malevolence: he conceived mischief, travailed with iniquity, brought forth falsehood — and all his expectations were blasted. John Wesley takes the metaphor of the deep design and the vigorous, restless endeavour that will not rest "till he have accomplished it."

The grammatical-historical witnesses draw the doctrine out of the figure. Charles Ellicott hears the poet's thought recurring to the calumniator whose sin has deserved all this divine wrath, and sees in it the truth that God's judgments are not arbitrary but follow naturally upon sin as its own consequence, the general figure of travail being elaborated in the two clauses of conception and delivery (Job 15:35). Keil and Delitzsch, on the same primary passage, note that man brings forth what he has conceived and reaps what he has sown, so that in the sin of his enemies David already sees their self-destruction; and they remark the singular order, that travail is named before pregnancy, since the word here means to be in the pangs, not to conceive.

The puritan-evangelical voices complete the picture. Matthew Henry describes the sinner's head, with its politics, conceiving mischief and laying the plot deep, while his heart travails with the malice it is hatching against the people of God; yet when it comes to the birth, it is falsehood — a cheat upon himself, a lie in his right hand, bringing forth nothing but wind and stubble and death. Charles Spurgeon sees three graphic strokes in the verse: the woman in travail, full of pangs till her evil intent be executed; the unhallowed conception, for "the devil has had doings with him"; and the progeny worthy of its father, whose name of old was the father of lies, so that the birth does not belie the parent. The witnesses do not divide: the wicked man labours mightily and is delivered only of a lie, and the mischief he conceives against the righteous turns, in the very bearing of it, to his own confusion.
15:
The figure shifts from the birth-pangs to the hunter's snare, and the witnesses follow the wicked man as he digs his own destruction — "he made a pit, and digged it, and is fallen into the ditch which he made." The reformed John Gill notes simply that he dug the pit and made it large and capacious to answer his purpose, only to tumble into it himself. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fills in the scene: the enemy determined David's destruction and laid his plans with much artifice, executing them with zeal, and when he supposed the grave of David dug, he fell into it himself. The metaphor, Clarke explains, is drawn from pits dug in the earth and lightly covered over with reeds, so that they cannot be told from solid ground, until the animal steps on them, the surface breaks, and he is taken; and he sets over the whole the word of Bishop Horne, that "all the world agrees to acknowledge the equity of that sentence which inflicts upon the guilty the punishment intended by them for the innocent."

The puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon dwells on the cunning and the stooping labour of it: the enemy was industrious in his mischief and did not fear to soil his own hands, willing to work in a ditch if only others might fall therein — for what mean things men will do to wreak revenge on the godly, hunting them like brute beasts, and not even with the fair chase given to the hare or the fox, but by secret entrapment, because they dare not meet them to the face. And then, he bids us look to the end of the scene, where the digger lies fallen in his own trench. Matthew Henry, expounding these same verses, draws the general rule: it is often remarkably true of those who contrive mischief against the people of God that, by the righteous hand of God, it is made to return upon their own heads, and what they designed for the shame of others proves their own confusion.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott turns to the history of the moral, comparing Abigail's word to David that his enemies' souls should be slung out as from the hollow of a sling (1 Sam. 25:29), and recalling that this very couplet was applied by Eusebius to the overthrow of Maxentius by Constantine, who, in building a bridge of boats across the Tiber, had prepared the very means of his own destruction. The witnesses do not divide: the pit is the emblem of a justice that needs no thunderbolt, but lets the plotter's own spade and his own weight bring him down into the grave he meant for another.
16:
What the pit pictured, the sixteenth verse states as a settled law of retribution — "his mischief shall return upon his own head, and his violent dealing shall come down upon his own pate." The reformed John Gill reads it as exactly that: whatever the wicked man conceived and devised in his mind and attempted to bring upon others shall fall back upon himself, a just judgment from heaven upon him. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, drawing these verses together, had made the same point the crown of the passage — that those who dig pits for the people of God prepare destruction for themselves by preparing themselves for destruction, loading themselves with guilt until their violence recoils, by the righteous hand of God, upon their own heads.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns to the old word "pate" and its Hebrew, kodkod, the crown or top of the head, the scalp; the phrase, he suggests, may point to knocking the criminal on the head to deprive him of life, and had scalping been known in those days he should have thought the reference might be to that barbarous custom. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott lingers over the same term, noting that "pate" was retained from Coverdale's translation and was common in the Elizabethan age — frequent in Shakespeare — and he reminds the reader once more of Abigail's blessing upon David, that the souls of his enemies should be flung away (1 Sam. 25:29), and of the way the couplet was fulfilled in history when the engine prepared for another's ruin became the ruin of him who built it.

Here the witnesses stand wholly together, and the verse gathers up the whole second half of the psalm. The sword whetted, the bow bent, the arrows made ready, the pit digged — all of it, the commentators agree, comes round at last not upon the innocent but upon the head that plotted it. Gill grounds the certainty in the justice of heaven; Henry in the moral constitution of things, whereby the sinner submits himself to his own corruptions; Clarke and Ellicott in the plain force of the ancient words for head and crown. The mischief does not merely fail; it returns, aimed now at its own author, so that the violent man is undone by the very violence he devised. It is the same equity Bishop Horne acknowledged at the pit, now spoken as a maxim: the stone rolls back upon him that rolled it, and the crown of the wicked man's head receives the blow he had measured out for another.
17:
The psalm that opened in fear closes in a vow of praise, and the witnesses gather to hear the slandered man become a singer — "I will praise the LORD according to his righteousness, and will sing praise to the name of the LORD most high." The reformed John Gill takes "according to his righteousness" of that righteousness displayed in vindicating the innocent and punishing the wicked, and finds a precedent in Moses and the children of Israel, who sang when Pharaoh, having ordered the Hebrew infants drowned, was himself with his host drowned in the Red Sea. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears David resolve to celebrate both God's justice and his mercy together, and unfolds "the name of the LORD most high" as the perfections of Jehovah who is above all; he even sets down the paraphrase of an old Scoto-English psalter — "song falls to joy; and he that sings well that name, his joy is more than I can tell" — for those who know God's name to be a strong tower have an inexpressible happiness.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, closing his own long comment, reads the verse as the fit end of the whole: we must praise the Lord according to his righteousness, giving him the glory both of the gracious protection under which he takes his afflicted people and of the just vengeance with which he pursues those that afflict them, singing to the praise of the Lord most high, who, when his enemies deal proudly, shows that he is above them. Charles Spurgeon too dwells on the joyful contrast in which all these psalms agree, exhibiting the blessedness of the righteous the more brightly against the misery of the wicked, the bright jewel sparkling on a black foil; the slandered one, whose harp was unstrung for a very little season, is now left sweeping its harmonious chords and mounting on their music to the third heaven of adoring praise.

The grammatical-historical witnesses let the verse close the psalm without dispute, Keil and Delitzsch simply carrying the reader to the concluding note of thanksgiving toward which the whole closing strophe had been moving. The witnesses do not divide: the movement of the psalm is complete, from the trembling trust of the opening cry to the settled song of the end, and the man who began by pleading "save me" ends by resolving to sing — his righteousness vindicated not by his own hand but by the righteousness of the God most high, whose name is both his refuge and his praise.
